title: Sessions vs JWTs and Token Revocation
lesson:
A server-side session stores state on the server (in a database or cache like Redis) and gives the client an opaque session ID, usually in a cookie. Every request looks the ID up, so the server can revoke a session instantly by deleting it, but every request needs a shared session store and a lookup on the hot path.

A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a signed, self-contained token carrying claims such as the user ID, roles, and an expiry. Any service holding the verification key can validate it without calling a central store, which scales well across many services. The tradeoff is revocation: since nothing is looked up, a validly signed token stays accepted until it expires, even if the user logs out or is banned. JWTs are signed, not encrypted by default, so anyone holding one can read its claims; never put secrets in them.

The usual compromise is short-lived access tokens (minutes) paired with a longer-lived refresh token stored and tracked server-side. When the access token expires, the client trades the refresh token for a new one, and the server can refuse if the session was revoked. Refresh-token rotation, issuing a new refresh token on each use and treating reuse of an old one as theft, limits damage from a leaked token. For instant revocation of access tokens, services can check a small denylist of revoked token IDs, which reintroduces a bit of shared state.

Choose based on needs: a single web app with strict logout and revocation requirements fits sessions well, while many independent services verifying identity cheaply fit short-lived JWTs well. Either way, store tokens in HttpOnly, Secure cookies where possible to reduce theft via cross-site scripting.

questions.prompt: What is the main drawback of a stateless, self-contained JWT access token?
options: It cannot carry a user ID
It is hard to revoke before its expiry because no server lookup occurs
It requires a database call on every request
questions.explanation: Validation uses only the signature and expiry, so a validly signed token stays accepted until it expires unless extra state is consulted.

questions.prompt: A signed JWT is encrypted by default, so its claims are hidden from the client holding it.
questions.explanation: Standard signed JWTs are only base64url-encoded and signed; anyone holding the token can read its claims.

questions.prompt: Short-lived access tokens are typically renewed using a longer-lived ____ token tracked on the server.
questions.explanation: The refresh token lets the server re-check session validity each time a new access token is issued.

questions.prompt: With refresh-token rotation, what should the server do if an already-used refresh token is presented again?
options: Accept it, since it was valid once
Treat it as possible theft and invalidate the token family or session
questions.explanation: Reuse of a rotated token suggests it was copied, so revoking the session limits the attacker's access.

questions.prompt: Order the steps when an access token expires in a short-lived-JWT-plus-refresh design.
items: Server issues a new access token (and rotated refresh token)
Client sends the refresh token to the auth server
API rejects the request because the access token expired
Server verifies the session has not been revoked
questions.explanation: The expired token is rejected, the client presents its refresh token, the server checks revocation, then issues fresh tokens.
